Sat, 29 Aug 2026 22:55:13 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1 https://beesayatv.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/cropped-09-32x32.png Roads – beesayatv https://beesayatv.com/ 32 32 Buot-Guila-Cabatbatan-Samboryo Trail Loop | Buot-Taup, Cebu City | 2026 GPX https://beesayatv.com/trails/buot-guila-cabatbatan-samboryo-trail-loop-buot-taup-cebu-city-2026-gpx/ Sat, 29 Aug 2026 09:32:12 +0000 https://beesayatv.com/?post_type=trail&p=1267 The Buot-Guila-Cabatbatan-Samboryo Trail Loop is a 12.75-kilometer loop through Buot-Taup, Guila-Guila, Babag Ridge, Dam-an, Cabatbatan, and Samboryo in Cebu City. I started near the suspended community bridge by the Barangay Buot-Taup Hall and initially followed the road toward Guila-Guila before climbing toward Babag Ridge and continuing through the mountain sections.

About 30% of the route was trail and 70% unpaved or concrete road, with moderate shade and many stores near the communities. I did this hike in August 2026 on a cloudy-sunny morning, and the trail was dry, with very few insects and almost no human traffic once I reached the high mountain sections.

Trail Snapshot

MILD
DocumentedAugust 2026
Distance12.75 km (Loop)

This 12.75km route begins at 174 m, climbs steadily through rolling terrain before a steep push to a peak elevation of 552 m around the 5 km mark, and then transitions into undulating ridge lines and sustained descents back down to 170 m.

Duration4-5 hrs
WaterAt least 2 liters
ShadeModerate
Surface30% trail, 70% road

Along the 13.1 km Buot–Guila–Cabatbatan route, the Smart network provided intermittent connectivity with coverage available for 75% of the recorded points (46.7% LTE) and 25% complete dead zones, maintaining generally weak signal quality that averaged -120.3 dBm.

GPXWikiloc

Forecast data: Open-Meteo

Access

I parked my motorcycle near the suspended bridge by the Barangay Buot-Taup Hall. There was no parking fee, and the road to the area was concrete. Public transportation was limited, while habal-habal and private vehicle access were available.

Because the loop exits back at the bridge, I first had to hike about 3.4 kilometers toward Guila-Guila. From there, I passed through a small hillside community and relied on directions from friendly locals to find the way.

Why this trail is rated Mild

✓ Mostly clear trail with occasional navigation awareness required
✓ Moderate hiking distance
✓ Sustained but manageable climbs or descents
✓ Some isolated sections between communities
✓ Limited turnaround or exit options

On this trail: bridge • cliff • farmland • forest • ridge • roads

Route Description

The ascent began immediately after the Guila-Guila hillside community and continued steadily toward Babag Ridge. Some sections were already being reclaimed by thick vegetation despite the recent Pamutan Trailfest 2026, and I noted that these portions could become difficult to follow within a few months.

Near the approach to Babag Ridge, farming activity kept the pathways clearer and more maintained. I then continued descending through the mountain sections toward Dam-an and Cabatbatan before ascending again toward Samboryo.

Along the way, I passed hillside farms and roadside plantings of cassava, corn, eggplant, and banana. Several concrete spring catchments had also been built across the agricultural areas for irrigation.

Two large cows blocked the pathway at one point, so I had to negotiate my way around them. I also passed two sections with heavy tree canopies that gave solid shade: one after Babag Ridge toward Dam-an and another near Samboryo on the way back toward Buot-Taup.

Trail Conditions

The trail was dry during my hike. Shade coverage was moderate overall, with the two heavily canopied sections providing more substantial cover. I encountered only a few insects throughout the route.

Stores were common near the communities, while the higher mountain sections had very few structures. Most houses were concentrated along the main roads on the lower hillsides.

Notes

I encountered dense groups of dogs near residential areas, but the open mountain sections were completely clear of animals. Human traffic was also limited: I met locals during the initial ascent in Guila-Guila and around the road crossings toward Dam-an, Cabatbatan, and Samboryo, but saw no other people on the high mountain trail.

Several stretches had moderate to high cliff exposure, although thick foliage largely hid the drop-offs. The route also had two large cows occupying the trail during my passage.

The descent toward Samboryo also showed how the route changes when approached from the opposite direction. From Buot-Taup toward Samboryo, the same section would involve a sustained climb on a narrow, rocky track.

]]> Inayagan-Cantao-an-Pangilatan Peak Community Trail Loop | Cantao-an, Naga City | 2026 GPX https://beesayatv.com/trails/inayagan-cantao-an-pangilatan-peak-community-trail-loop-cantao-an-naga-city-2026-gpx/ Fri, 21 Aug 2026 05:37:09 +0000 https://beesayatv.com/?post_type=trail&p=1235 The Pangilatan Peak Loop is a 5.26 km loop hike located across Inayagan and Cantao-an in Naga City. I followed a route that began high on the mountain, descended toward the Metro Cebu Expressway, and circled back up past several rural communities to reach the peak.

The hike was characterized by a long, steep initial descent over fine scree and sharp rock, followed by road walking through active construction areas and local settlements. A morning haze hung across the valley during this sunny hike, which I completed in August 2026.

Trail Snapshot

MILD
DocumentedAugust 2026
Distance5.26 km (Loop)

This 5.26 km loop hike features an overall elevation gain of approximately 317 m, ranging between 38 m and 313 m in altitude, with smoothed maximum grades reaching roughly +28% uphill and -26% downhill, and its toughest climb occurring on the sustained ascent to Pangilatan Peak between kilometer 3.6 and 4.2.

Duration2.5 - 3 hrs
WaterAt least 2 liters
ShadeLimited
Surface60% trail, 40% road

The trail maintains predominantly usable LTE coverage fluctuating between 1 and 4 bars to support voice calls, messaging, and online navigation, punctuated by an isolated complete dead zone and brief drops to 2G/GSM where data connectivity is lost.

GPXWikiloc

Forecast data: Open-Meteo

Access

I started at the foot of Pangilatan Peak, where motorcycle parking was available without a fee. The jump-off point was accessible by concrete road and could be reached by private vehicle. Public transportation to the area was limited, though habal-habal services were available.

Why this trail is rated Mild

✓ Moderate hiking distance
✓ Sustained but manageable climbs or descents
✓ Some isolated sections between communities
✓ Moderate route commitment
✓ Limited turnaround or exit option

On this trail: cliff • forest • peak • roads • valley

Route Description

Since the jump-off point sits on top of the mountain, I began with a continuous 1.22 km descent toward the lowlands. The footpath was covered with loose scree and razor-sharp rock surfaces, requiring careful footing on the way down.

At the bottom of the hill, the trail intersected the active Metro Cebu Expressway project, where I walked through dirt, dust, and mud near large construction machinery. After passing the construction corridor, the route turned uphill along the road, leading through several residential communities before returning to Pangilatan Peak to complete the loop.

Trail Conditions

The weather remained sunny throughout the morning, and trail surfaces stayed completely dry. Tree cover was limited, leaving most of the route exposed to the sun. Small local stores were open near the communities along the back half of the loop, though carrying at least 2 liters of water was necessary.

I ran into high insect activity along the footpaths, and the crowd consisted mostly of locals, along with a few joggers and hikers near Pangilatan Peak. Approximately 60% of the route followed dirt and rock trails, while the remaining 40% consisted of roads.

Additional Notes

Dogs were present in large numbers along the trails and near the settlements, making a trekking pole especially helpful both for stability on the loose rock and for keeping animals at a distance. Although the sweeping valley landscape remained broad and open, morning haze kept the view from looking as crisp as on my previous visit.

Early morning hikers and joggers mostly used the concrete road leading to the peak, while others continued onto the mountain path to finish their hike.

I followed well-used footpaths through scattered hillside homes, open grasslands, and quiet countryside before returning to the starting point.

The route featured rolling climbs and descents instead of one sustained ascent, while the mostly open terrain provided views toward Naga, Minglanilla, and Talisay. Although navigation remained straightforward for most of the hike, the moderate distance and repeated elevation changes made it more physically demanding than a typical beginner trail. I completed this hike in July 2026.

MILD
DocumentedJuly 2026
Distance7.61 km (Loop)

This 7.61 km loop hike features a filtered elevation gain of approximately 261 m, ranging between 29 m and 223 m in altitude, with smoothed maximum grades reaching roughly +28% uphill and -27% downhill, and its toughest climb occurring on the steep approach between kilometer 1.1 and 1.7.

Duration2.5 - 3 hrs
WaterAt least 1 liter
ShadeLimited
Surface60% trail, 40% road
GPXWikiloc

Access

I started near the jump-off, where motorcycle parking was available along the roadside without a parking fee. The trailhead was accessible by concrete road, and private vehicles could reach the area. Public transportation was limited, although habal-habal services were available.

Why this trail is rated Mild

✓ Mostly clear trail with occasional navigation awareness required
✓ Moderate hiking distance
✓ Sustained but manageable climbs or descents
✓ Some isolated sections between communities
✓ Assistance may require additional time to reach

On this trail: cliff • roads • stairs • viewpoint

Route Description

I began by following a well-trodden community trail that climbed through scattered hillside homes and open grasslands. Early in the hike, several sections opened up to views of Naga, Minglanilla, and Talisay before the route continued across rolling terrain with pockets of vegetation. Throughout the hike, I regularly passed signs of everyday community life, even in the quieter sections.

After reaching Campagao Peak, I continued around the loop before descending toward Manduang. Much of the descent followed a long concrete staircase, making navigation straightforward until I returned to the jump-off. I also passed several dogs near homes and gave them plenty of space while walking through the communities.

Trail Conditions

The weather remained sunny throughout my hike. Most of the route was exposed with limited shade, and the trail stayed dry during my visit. Mobile signal remained available from start to finish, while stores were present along the route near the communities. I mostly encountered local residents rather than other hikers, and insect activity was noticeably higher during this hike.

Additional Notes

Houses and small settlements appeared along much of the route, so I rarely felt far from the community. Farming activity was limited during my visit, although the landscape was clearly agricultural. Some sections had moderate cliff exposure, but vegetation reduced the feeling of exposure while walking.

A hiking stick can also be useful when passing the territorial dogs commonly found along the trail.

]]> Mini Switzerland | Campinsa, Talisay | 2026 GPX https://beesayatv.com/trails/mini-switzerland-campinsa-talisay-2026-gpx/ Wed, 01 Jul 2026 07:41:00 +0000 https://beesayatv.com/?post_type=trail&p=416 Mini Switzerland is a documented 6 km loop hike in Campinsa and Manipis, Talisay City. I followed a route that combined cemented paths, open countryside, hillside trails, and quiet mountain roads before returning to the starting point.

The hike began with a long downhill walk before transitioning into rolling terrain and a steady uphill climb back to the jump-off. Navigation remained straightforward throughout, and I completed this hike in April 2026.

Trail Snapshot

EASY
DocumentedApril 2026
Distance6 km (Loop)
Duration3 - 3.5 hrs
WaterAt least 2 liters
ShadeLimited

I started in Campinsa, where motorcycle parking was available along the roadside without a parking fee. The jump-off was accessible by concrete road, and private vehicles could reach the area. Public transportation was very limited, although habal-habal services were available.

✓ Easy-to-follow trail
✓ No technical climbing required

Route Description

I began by descending a long flight of cemented stairs before joining Manipis Road. From there, the route continued across open hillside trails and rolling terrain leading toward Windy Hills Campsite. Navigation stayed simple throughout, and several sections opened up to views of the surrounding mountains.

After completing the downhill and rolling portions of the loop, I started the steady climb back to Campinsa. Although none of the climbs were technical, the continuous uphill section marked the most demanding part of the return.

Trail Conditions

The weather remained sunny throughout my hike. Most of the route was exposed with very little shade, while the trail stayed dry during my visit. Walking conditions could become muddy after rain. I did not find any stores along the route, and mobile signal remained strong near the jump-off before disappearing farther into the hike. I encountered no other hikers and noticed very few insects.

Additional Notes

Part of the route passed through an active road construction area during my visit in April 2026.

I followed a straightforward community route with steady climbs, rolling farmland, mountain views, and quiet rural roads before returning to the starting point.

Although navigation remained simple throughout, the continuous ascents and longer distance made the hike more physically demanding than the terrain itself. I completed this hike in June 2026.

Duration2-3 hrs

GPXWikiloc

Access

I started near Camp 7 National High School, where motorcycle parking was available along the roadside without a parking fee. The jump-off was accessible by a mix of concrete and dirt roads, and private vehicles could reach the area. Public transportation was limited, although habal-habal services were available. The parking area was about 2 km before the junction leading to Canapnapan 2.

Why this trail is rated Mild

✓ Mostly easy-to-follow trail
✓ Basic hiking experience recommended
✓ Moderate physical effort required

On this trail: farmland • ridge • roads • rolling hills • viewpoint

Route Description

I began by following community roads and trails toward Canapnapan 2 before continuing through Canapnapan 3, Cabanbanan, and Upper Camp 8. The route passed rolling farmland, open countryside, and several residential areas where I frequently met local residents. Navigation stayed straightforward from start to finish, with the steady climbs providing the main physical challenge rather than any technical terrain.

As I continued around the loop, several sections opened up to wide views of the surrounding mountains before the trail gradually returned to the starting point. I also passed many dogs along the route, especially near homes, and kept a comfortable distance while walking through the communities.

Trail Conditions

The weather remained sunny throughout my hike. Much of the route was exposed with limited shade, although I found several stores whenever I passed through local communities. The trail stayed dry during my visit but could become very muddy after rainfall. Mobile signal was strong near the start before becoming intermittent in some areas. I encountered many people throughout the hike and noticed only a few insects.

Additional Notes

This route passed through established communities rather than remote mountain terrain, and the locals I met, especially the children, were friendly and helpful. Hiking the loop in the opposite direction would turn the section from the road junction toward Cabanbanan into a long, continuous climb.

A hiking stick or trekking pole can also be useful for anyone who is uncomfortable walking past the many dogs found along the route.

I followed a route through Camp 7, Lubas, Ylaya, and Camp 8, passing a man-made forest, farmland, and rolling countryside before returning to the starting point.

The hike featured repeated gradual climbs and descents across mostly open terrain, with long views of the surrounding hills. Although navigation remained straightforward, the accumulated elevation gain and extended exposed sections made the hike more physically demanding than the terrain alone suggested. I completed this hike in May 2026.

Distance10 km (Loop)
Duration4-5 hrs
WaterAt least 2 liters

Route Description

I began the hike by walking through a man-made forest, which made for a comfortable warm-up before the trail opened into farmland and rolling countryside. From there, I continued across a series of gradual climbs and descents connecting Camp 7, Lubas, Ylaya, and Camp 8. The route remained easy to follow throughout, although the repeated elevation changes gradually added to the effort as the hike progressed.

Later in the hike, longer downhill sections marked much of the return. Even though none of the individual climbs were particularly steep, the combination of distance and continuous rolling terrain made the final kilometers feel more demanding.

Trail Conditions

The weather stayed sunny throughout my hike. Most of the trail was exposed with very little shade, while the ground remained dry during my visit. The trail could become muddy after rain. Mobile signal was strong near the trailhead before becoming weak or disappearing farther along the route. I did not find any stores during the hike, encountered only a few other people, and noticed very few insects.

Additional Notes

The opening section through the man-made forest provided a gradual start before the trail entered more exposed farmland. Because the route passed through working agricultural areas, I never felt isolated during the hike.

]]> Alpaco Trail Loop | Pinamungahan / Alpaco, Naga City | 2026 GPX https://beesayatv.com/trails/alpaco-trail-loop-pinamungahan-alpaco-naga-city-2026-gpx/ Wed, 24 Jun 2026 14:13:01 +0000 https://beesayatv.com/?post_type=trail&p=125 The Alpaco Trail Loop is a documented 12 km loop hike in Pinamungahan, Cebu. I started near the trail leading to Veloso Lake before continuing through Purok Hoybesan, Bandilaan, and Alpaco, eventually returning to the starting point.

Around 80% of the route followed concrete roads, while the remaining sections used community trails and footpaths. Navigation stayed straightforward throughout the hike, although the longer distance and extended exposed sections made it more demanding than the terrain itself suggested. I completed this hike in June 2026.

Trail Snapshot

MILD
DocumentedJune 2026
Distance12 km (Loop)
Duration3-4 hrs
WaterAt least 2 liters
ShadeModerate
Surface20% trail, 80% road
GPXWikiloc

Forecast data: Open-Meteo

Access

I started near the trail going up to Veloso Lake, where motorcycle parking was available along the roadside without a parking fee. The access road to the jump-off was concrete. Private vehicles could reach the area, although four-wheel vehicles could not continue along the narrow access trail toward the lake, leaving a short walk to reach it. Public transportation was very limited, but habal-habal services were available. Besides my approach, Veloso Lake can also be reached from Sibago and Alpaco.

Why this trail is rated Mild

✓ Mostly easy-to-follow trail
✓ Occasional people encountered
✓ Longer hiking distance
✓ Long exposed sections with little shade
✓ Limited turnaround points

On this trail: forest • lake • roads • viewpoint

Route Description

I began by heading toward Veloso Lake before continuing along the loop through Purok Hoybesan, Bandilaan, and Alpaco. The route alternated between community trails and long stretches of concrete road, making navigation easy for most of the day. Although Veloso Lake marked the beginning of my hike, it was only a short side trip before the main loop continued through the surrounding communities.

As I moved farther along the route, I passed several residential areas where I met friendly locals and had a number of pleasant conversations. Pig-raising areas appeared along some sections, and the smell was noticeable as I walked through them. I also ran into several dogs near homes. None of the dogs I encountered were friendly, and most behaved territorially, so I gave them plenty of space while passing.

Trail Conditions

The morning was cloudy during my hike. Most of the route remained exposed with limited shade, especially along the concrete roads. The trail surface alternated between dry and muddy sections, while mobile signal started out strong before becoming intermittent later in the hike. I found several stores whenever the route passed through communities, and I only saw a small number of other people throughout the day. Insects were minimal.

Additional Notes

There are three documented approaches to Veloso Lake. I used the shortest approach, which requires a brief walk because the narrow access trail is unsuitable for four-wheel vehicles, although a few motorcycles continue farther. Since most of this loop follows concrete roads, I noticed that habal-habal drivers regularly passed through the area, making it possible to leave the hike early if needed. The longer distance and limited turnaround points were the main factors that added commitment to an otherwise straightforward route.
